items.text: (ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS) BILL—
In Committee—
21 Aug 2012 Motions 4527
TUESDAY, 21 AUGUST 2012
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Prayers.
MOTIONS
New Zealand Defence Force—Deaths of Corporal Luke Tamatea, Lance Corporal
Jacinda Baker, and Private Richard Harris in Afghanistan

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I seek leave to move a motion without
notice on the incident on Sunday, 19 August in the Bamian Province of Afghanistan,
which tragically claimed the lives of three New Zealand soldiers.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There
is none.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I move, That this House express its deep sympathy and
condolences to the families, friends, and mili tary colleagues of the three New Zealand
soldiers killed in Afghanistan on 19 August. It is with profound sorrow and also a deep
sense of shock that just 1 week after this House passed a motion expressing its
condolences on the deaths of Lance Corporal  Pralli Durrer and Lance Corporal Rory
Malone in Afghanistan we should find ourselv es here again paying our respects to three
of their colleagues. On Sunday morning Co rporal Luke Tamatea, Lance Corporal
Jacinda Baker, and Private Richard Harris were travelling in a convoy on the road to
Romero in Bamian. They were in the last of the four Humvees, and were driving it in
order to seek medical assistance for one of their colleagues travelling in the same
convoy. At 9.21 a.m. their Humvee was hit by a massive improvised explosive device.
The explosion was not survivable. These thr ee New Zealanders, who were serving their
country so loyally and so well, were killed instantly.
In this House last week my colleague De puty Prime Minister Bill English said that
the Defence Force families knew there were risks in the job, but that did not make it any
easier when the knock at the door that they  hoped would never come did come. On
Sunday it came for the families and friends  of Luke Tamatea, Jacinda Baker, and
Richard Harris, and for their colleagues in the Defence Force, and, indeed, for all New
Zealanders. It is, of course, the families and friends of the three fallen soldiers who bear
the loss most acutely, and to them we extend our deep sympathy. At this time this
House also thinks of the other families who ha ve lost soldiers in this conflict, and we
know that this will have renewed their pain. We are mindful, too, that  four of the five
soldiers lost in the past fortnight were from the 2/1 st Battalion, based at Burnham. Our
thoughts are with that regiment in particular.
In the last couple of days tr ibutes have been paid to L uke Tamatea, Jacinda Baker,
and Richard Harris, and in that way we have put names and personalities to the toll. The
three were different, but they shared characteristics in common with other New Zealand
servicemen and women who have served a nd who continue to se rve in Afghanistan.
They were loyal, they were brave, and they  were hard-working members of a team that
always looked out for each other. It would not have been possible to ask more of them.
Our mission and mandate in Afghanistan has been to provide sufficient security to
allow the reconstruction to occur, which has significantly improved the lives of local
people. Through the efforts of our brave soldie rs, we have seen in the Bamian Province
the mortality rate for children under 5 halved, and maternal deaths are a quarter of the
2002 levels. Bamian University is now a multi-faculty institution with 2,700 students
this year, of which 15 percent are female. N early half of all primary school children
4528 Motions 21 Aug 2012
going to school in the Bamian Province are no w girls. This is a record of which our
servicemen and women can be extremely proud.
At the same time soldiers like Luke Tama tea, Jacinda Baker, and Richard Harris
have been serving New Zealand. Their effort is our contribution to an international force
mandated by the United Nations. We have contributed in a way that is built on the finest
traditions of the New Zealand military over generations. We have enhanced our
reputation as a defence force that is totally committed to the task, even when the
conditions are difficult or dangerous. As I have made cl ear in the past couple of days,
the Government is committed to withdrawing fro m Afghanistan in the first part of next
year, and we will continue to work towards the best way to do this. When we leave, it
will be done in a way that honours the sacrific e and effort New Zealanders have made
for a country that is not thei r own. Bamian is a better pl ace for Luke Tamatea, Jacinda
Baker, and Richard Harris having been ther e. We are proud of them, we mourn them,
and we wish that they rest in peace.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: A week ago today at this very
moment we stood to remember the lives of  Lance Corporal Pralli Durrer and Lance
Corporal Rory Malone. We paid tribute to  their commitment, their dedication, and the
sacrifice they made for their country. We celebrated their achievements in life and we
mourned their loss in death. We never imagin ed that we would be  standing here today
to pay our respects to three of their colleagues, who have also had their lives cut brutally
short in the service of their country. It is not right or fair, but we must put those feelings
aside to come together to express our sorrow  at the loss of thr ee young Kiwis, who will
never get the chance to fulfil the promise and the potential that their lives offered.
At the age of 31, Corporal Luke Tamatea ha d already given so much. He had a long
history of serving his country in Timor-Leste and the Solomons, and he had helped with
the tsunami recovery in Sumatra. He was on his second deployment to Afghanistan. He
was a relaxed, easygoing guy who is remembered fondly in hi s home town of Te Teko,
near Kawerau, as a mountain of a man, and, of course, as a father.
Lance Corporal Jacinda Baker joined the army as a medic. She was in Afghanistan to
take care of others and was doing just that  when she died. She had already received a
commendation in 2008 for her professionalism a nd courage. Jacinda Baker is the first
female Kiwi soldier to be killed in acti on since we entered Afgha nistan, and the first
New Zealand woman to die in conflict since the Viet Nam War.
Private Richard Harris was just 21. He ha d already served one stint in Afghanistan.
He was a keen, sporty guy who enjoyed his lif e in the army and had a bright future
ahead of him. He was far too young to di e. Our thoughts and pray ers are today with
their families and friends.
We have lost five of our soldiers in just 2 weeks. The lives of 10 Kiwi military
personnel have been ended by violence in Afghanistan during our 9 years’ commitment
there. The loss is so great, it is difficult for families, friends, colleagues, and our nation
to bear. We ask ourselves whether it is too hi gh a price. It is the price that we ask the
members of our armed forces to be prepared to pay whenever they enter a conflict zone.
Their courage and willingness to risk their lives doing their duty in  the service of our
country is an inspiration to us all.
We should not forget that our efforts in Af ghanistan have made a real difference to
the lives of the people there. Children safely  attend school, they are vaccinated against
disease, wells and village water supplie s have been hooked up, and bridges and
hospitals rebuilt. Hundreds—perhaps thousa nds—of Afghan people would not be alive
today if not for our presence. That is all th anks to the efforts of our soldiers. That
contribution will never be forgotten.
21 Aug 2012 Motions 4529
We have done all that has been asked of us by the international community, and, as a
small nation, we have now done all we can. It is time to hand the country back to its
own people and its own police forces and s ecurity forces. It must be an orderly
transition, and it will take months to co mplete the handover to the Afghan National
Police and to withdraw our forces and our equipment, but it is right, after almost a
decade, that the end of our commitment in Afghanistan be firmly in sight. We should
leave the Afghans with the best possible start.
We thank all of the New Zealanders who have served there on our behalf and who
have helped rebuild that fragile country in their many different roles. We recognise their
bravery and their willingness to do their best to give others a better life.
But today we stand with the families and friends of Luke Tamatea, Jacinda Baker,
and Richard Harris as they come to terms w ith the shock of losing their loved ones. We
cannot comprehend the depth of your grief,  but all New Zealanders want you to know
that you are not alone at this most difficult time. You are in our thoughts and prayers.
May your loved ones rest in peace.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: The Green Party stands once again to
acknowledge the sacrifice made by New Zeal and soldiers. We pay tribute to Lance
Corporal Jacinda Baker, Priv ate Richard Harris, and Corpor al Luke Tamatea, members
of the provincial reconstructi on team in Afghanistan. This is a painful moment. Ten
New Zealand soldiers have now died in Afghanistan since 2010. This is the greatest loss
of life and injury in active New Zealand se rvice since Viet Nam. The loss is felt
throughout the country.
Around these walls are various battle wr eaths and plaques carved in wood. The 12
commemorating First World War battles were installed in 1918. The remaining 18
plaques commemorate the South African war,  the Second World War, and subsequent
events, which were added in the 1960s. Perhaps Afghanistan will be added. If it is, it
will stand as a reminder that almost 100 years after the first battles depicted here, we
have not learnt how to tame warfare.
The sacrifice of these three New Zealande rs, along with the two whom we honoured
this same moment last wee k, and the other five who have  also fallen in Afghanistan,
demands that we re-examine our beliefs, our values, our institutions, and our methods of
relating between societies in the 21 st century. We in New Zeal and and all of us around
the world must reassess what it will take to ensure that human conflict and the
contestation of ideas are handled with great er dignity and in peace. That is the real
tribute we can pay these young people and the families they leave behind.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: On behalf of New Zealand First I wish to
express our greatest sympathy to the family, wh ānau, friends, and comrades of these
brave soldiers: Corporal Luke Tamatea fr om Kawerau, Lance Corporal Jacinda Baker
from Christchurch, and Private Richard Harri s from Pukekohe. It is with great sorrow
that within the short space of 2 weeks we  are mourning the loss of more New Zealand
soldiers in Afghanistan. They died in the service of their countr y, undertaking a short,
15-kilometre road journey to take a sick mate for medical treatment.
This is the first time since the Viet Na m War that we have mourned the loss of a
woman killed in action. It has also not been since the height of th e Viet Nam War, in
1968, 1969, and 1970, that we have lost so many soldiers in such a short space of time. I
feel great sorrow for the latest loss of liv es and for those who gr ieve for them, and I
know how their loved ones are feeling this week, having lost my brother in Viet Nam in
1969. The pain of the tragic loss never goe s away, but the families and friends can
always be incredibly proud of  the ultimate sacrifice their loved one made in the service
of their country.
4530 Motions 21 Aug 2012
New Zealand soldiers working in the provinc ial reconstruction team have carried out
beneficial work in Bamian Province, which has greatly improved the lives and safety of
civilians there. We admire all the selfless work  that these soldiers carried out to help
others and we acknowledge that  it takes great courage and bravery to serve in such a
war-torn area as Afghanistan. This is a time for our nation to remember those whom we
have lost and pay them the tribute they greatly deserve. May they rest in peace.

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker.
Ka tū ake au ki te tautoko i ng ā mihi o ng ā rangatira, ngā kaiārahi, ngā kaikōrero o ngā
rōpū o te Whare nei kua tukuna atu ō rātou poroporoaki ki te tokotoru, otirā, ngā mihi ki
ngā wh ānau, n ā reira, t ēnā koutou. Ki ng ā toa tokotoru o T ūmatauenga, ki a Luke
Douglas Tamatea, e 31 ōna tau, nō Te Teko, i T āmaki-makau-rau e noho ana. Tokowh ā
āna tamariki i Kawerau, e 12 ōna tau i te pakanga i Te Taua o T ūmatauenga. Ki a
Jacinda Francis Elyse Baker, e 26 ōna tau, nō Ōtautahi, he tākuta tāna mahi. I tērā tau ka
tohua ia ki te m ētara toa, Chief of Army’s Commendation for courage. Ko ia te h ōia
wahine tuatahi o Aotearoa i mate i te paka nga i Afghanistan. Ki a Richard Lee Harris, e
21 ōna tau, n ō Ngāpuhi ki Hokianga, ki Puket ī me Ng āti Maru. I Pukekohe ia e noho
ana. Ka takoto ia ki Piki-te-Aroha marae, takiw ā o R āhiri ki te Hokianga. N ō te Ope
Tuatahi me te Ope Tuarua hoki o te R oyal New Zealand Infantry Regiment r ātou katoa,
e mahi ana m ā te Taua Whakatika Takiw ā i Bamian. E 145 ng ā mema o taua r ōpū, e 9
tau rātau i reira. I haere katoa atu ēnei hōia ki Bamian i te Āperira, Paenga-whāwhā, o
tēnei tau.
I mate i te pah ū nui, he mea huna n ā te Taliban i te rori, i te takiw ā o Do Abe, e tata
ana ki te wāhi i mate ai ō rātou hoa tokorua i ng ā wiki tata nei. I te w ā o te pahūtanga, i
te kawe r ātou i t ētahi hoa h ōia ki te h ōhipera. E meatia ana, n ā te pai o ng ā mahi a ō
tātou hōia ki te whakapakari i ng ā iwi i Bamian te take, i tino p īrangi ai te Taliban kia
patua. Nō reira, e mihi ana au ki tērā rōpū tauā mō ā rātou mahi toa i reira.
Ko te tikanga, ka hoki mai ngā hōia katoa ki Aotearoa a te Paenga-whāwhā o te tau e
tū mai nei. T ērā pea ka tae ki te w ā, e t ū ai ng ā iwi o reira i runga i t ō rātou ake
rangatiratanga, waiho mā rātou anō rātou e whakapakari.
Nā reira koutou, hoki wairua mai ki a m ātou i Aotearoa nei. Hoki wairua mai koutou
ki te whānau o ngā hōia kia taea e ō koutou hoa, te tangi, mihi, poroporoaki i a koutou.
Kia ūhia ngā kōrero ki runga i a koutou. Kia ringihia ng ā roimata me ngā hūpē ki runga
i a koutou. Kia whakang āwari ai i t ēnā hīkoi ki roto i ō koutou wh ānau. Kia takoto ai
koutou i ō koutou k āinga t ūturu, i waenga i ō koutou wh ānau, hap ū, iwi. Kia mihia
koutou, kia poroporoakihia koutou. Nā reira koutou, haere, haere atu rā.
Ki ngā mātua, tīpuna, whānau o te tokotoru nei, ēhara tēnei i te mahi m āmā kia kite
ai ngā mātua i ō rātou tamariki e hinga mai ana i mua i t ō rātou matenga. Nā reira, tēnā
koutou kia kaha, anei m ātou o te Whare P āremata e tautoko ana i a koutou i t ēnei wā
pōuri ō koutou. N ā reira, koutou ki a koutou ng ā mate, ā, tātou te hunga ora ki a t ātou
tēnā koutou, kei raro.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. I rise to endorse  the acknowledgments of party leaders,
leading figures, and spokespersons of this H ouse who expressed their farewell tributes
to the three, and, indeed, thei r condolences to the families, and so thank you. To the
three warriors of the New Zealand Army: Luke Douglas Tamatea, aged 31, of Te Teko,
who lived in Auckland, has four children in  Kawerau, and served in the army for 12
years; Jacinda Francis Elyse Baker, aged 26, of  Christchurch, a medic, who received a
Chief of Army’s Commendation for courage last year, and is the first New Zealand
female combat casualty in Afghanistan; and Richard Lee Harris, aged 21, a Ng āpuhi
from Hokianga, Puketī, and a Ngāti Maru, who lived in Pukekohe and will lie in state at
Piki-te-Aroha Marae at R āhiri, Hokianga. All three were from the 2/1 st Battalion of the
Royal New Zealand Infantry Regiment and were part of a 145-strong provincial
21 Aug 2012 Motions 4531
reconstruction team stationed in the province of Bamian for 9 years. All these troops
went to Bamian in April this year.
The trio died in a massive explosion from  a bomb concealed by the Taliban on the
road to Do Abe, close to the area where two of their fellow soldiers were killed in
recent weeks. At the time of the explosion, th ey were taking a fellow soldier to hospital.
It has been stated that because our troops were doing such a sterling job to improve the
lives of the people of Bamian, the Taliban really wanted to target and kill them. So I pay
a tribute to that troop for their courageous efforts there.
According to what has been planned, the expected withdrawal of all New Zealand
soldiers is set for April next year. By t hat time perhaps the people of Afghanistan would
have regained their independence and ability to  make their own decisions. In terms of
how best they can improve their lives, leave that for them to determine.
Therefore I say to you three, return in spirit to us here in New Zealand. Return
spiritually to the family of the army so  that your fellow soldiers can mourn,
acknowledge, and farewell you three. It will  enable you to be shrouded with speeches
and have outpourings of tears and mucus cast over you. Those elements will ease the
journey back for each of you to your own fa milies and to lie in stat e in your place of
birth among your family, subtribe, and tribe.  And it is there that they will acknowledge
and farewell you. So depart, go forth, goodbye.
To you, the parents, ancestors, and families of this trio, this is not an easy situation
for parents to see their children predecease them. Hence I say to you be strong. We, the
members of the House of Representatives, support you at this time of your sadness.
To you, the dead, I say unto you, remain there among your own, and we, the living, I
acknowledge us all and resume my seat.]

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: Hoi anō, hei kōrero tuatahi me mihi atu ki
a koutou katoa e tuku poroporoaki ki a r ātou ngā rangatira kua mate atu ki t ērā taha o te
ao. E tika ana ki a mihi atu ki ng ā mate i t ēnei w ā, haere, haere, haere. Koutou e ng ā
whānau e tatari tonu ana kia hoki mai ki te k āinga, e tika ana kia m ōhio ai koutou, anei
mātou katoa o roto o te P āremata, hākoa ko wai te tangata, ko t ēhea te p āti, e t ū kotahi
ana i roto i te pōuritanga kei runga i a koutou i tēnei wā.
[So, to begin with, I acknowledge you all who made tributes of farewell to them, the
chiefly ones who died on the other side of the world. It is fitting as well at this point in
time that I say to the deaths, farewell, de part, and journey on. To  you, the families who
are still waiting for their return home, it is fit ting that you know that all of us here in
Parliament, regardless who it is and which party it is, stand as one with you in this hour
of sadness upon you.]
Last week a number of M āori MPs from different political parties debated a range of
issues on Native Affairs . Naturally, we all ha d our different opinion s on all of those
issues, except one: what to do about our troops  in Afghanistan. It wa s nice to hear that
on that one issue we were all singing from the same song sheet: bring the troops home.
I know that in this House it might seem inappropriate to be asking why we are at war
when our troops are dying. I do not want peopl e to think that asking questions here
today in any way challenges the sacrifice th at our troops have made, for some have
made the ultimate sacrifice. But I also know th at when we go to a tangi for one of our
whānau who has died in a car accident, or from  smoking, or from an act of violence, or
from anything else, we openly ask ourselves why they died, and whether or not there
was anything we could have  done to stop them dying. Toda y is no different. Today
people prepare for the return of their love d ones from Afghanistan. Today we all mourn
those who have died, both M āori and non-M āori, and we all share in the grief of their
whānau and their communities. Today is the righ t time to ask questions about why they
4532 Motions 21 Aug 2012
died, and whether or not ther e was anything we could ha ve done to stop them dying—
questions that some of the families of those still in Afghanistan want answered.
They are questions like why exactly it is that we are expected to stay the course when
that course has changed from one of recons truction to a more aggressive role. Are our
troops still involved in reconstr uction, or has that changed to  a more direct battle for
their survival? Why are we hearing that New Zealand vehicles are being stopped and
searched by the Taliban? Is that happening because neither New Zealand forces nor any
other coalition forces can guarantee security there any longer? When the Prime Minister
himself talks about the need to restore secu rity, is it because he  too has accepted what
everybody already knows—that security is deteriorating in Afghanistan? Is deteriorating
security the reason why the H ungarians refuse to patrol at  night, and is that why New
Zealand troops are being asked to take on a greater role there? Does the Government
accept that the deteriorating security status in Bamian and across the country means that
New Zealand need not commit itself to an Amer ican timetable of departure, and that we
are entirely within our rights as a sovereign nation to ensure the sa fety and security of
our own troops by withdrawi ng them from front-line action? When the Government
says that it does not want it  to look like the Taliban is forcing New Zealand out of
Afghanistan, surely it is not saying that it is willing to sacrifice New Zealand troops to
prove how staunch we are. When the Minister  of Defence confirmed last night that the
reports are true that the Taliban is now specifically targeting New Zealand troops, why
was he unable to say what additional secur ity is being provided for those troops? Can
somebody in the Government tell mothers and fathers at home why it is that the
Government has cut back on the resources for our remaining troops when they are under
greater threat now than they have ever been? And can somebody please tell us why we
have withdrawn the SAS at a time when their support is most desperately needed by our
own troops on the ground?
If the Government’s commitment to reducing funding, reduc ing resourcing, and
reducing the support levels for our troops in  Afghanistan is met by a declaration of
specific targeting of our remaining troops by the Taliban, then it is time to accept that
the reduction in overall securi ty of our forces on the ground presents our Government
with one of two simple choices: an immediate enhancement of the security for those on
the ground until such time as they can be withdrawn as soon as possible, or an
immediate withdrawal of all New Zealand troops from Afghanistan.
Hoi anō, hei whakakapi i taku k ōrero ēhara i te mea, hei takatakahia i ng ā mahi a te
Kāwanatanga ēngari, kia mihi atu ki ng ā wh ānau e tatari ana kia hoki tika mai ng ā
tūpāpaku o r ātou kia mate atu i t ērā o ng ā whenua. N ō reira e ng ā mate, haere koutou,
haere koutou, haere koutou. Huri t ū ki a t ātou te kanohi ora, t ātou e nohonoho nei, tena
koutou huri rauna, kia ora tātou katoa.
[So, to end my address, it is not as though I am walking all over Government action
but rather I am paying a tribute to families wa iting for the bodies of loved ones to come
directly back to them  from those lands over  there. And so to you, the dead, farewell,
depart, and move on. I turn to us, the living seated about here, to acknowledge you and
all of us throughout, thank you.]

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: It is with great sadness that I rise to speak on
behalf of the ACT Party on the loss of our th ree soldiers in Afghanistan: Corporal Luke
Tamatea, Lance Corporal Jacinda Baker, and Private Richard Harris. It is made all the
more difficult, is it not, when it was just this time last week that we paid tribute to two
other brother soldiers who lost their lives for the same cause. For the 2/1 st Battalion,
Royal New Zealand Infantry Regiment, based in  Burnham, it is five deaths in 2 weeks.
It is a credit to our country that we con tinue to have brave men and women who are
prepared to step up and defend democracy at  any corner of the world. I recall again
21 Aug 2012 Motions 4533
those words that are written high above the gates on entry to the infantry base at

items.speaker: Burnham
items.text: “Remember that prosperity can only be for the free, and that freedom is the
sure possession of those alone who have the courage to defend it.” I cannot imagine the
thoughts that will be in the minds of their fellow soldiers still on the ground in Bamian
Province, but we here today want them to  know that we back home continually think
about them, we care about them, and we greatly value their brave work. To the fallen.
Our heartfelt sympathy goes out to their families, to their friends, and to the military at
this very difficult time.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Up and down New Zealand in
every little village and town the centrepiece is a war memorial upon which are displayed
the names of those who have died in battles past. Many of us, I suspect, have looked
upon those names and wondered about the people who are but chiselled memories there.
What were they like? What were their aspirations? What were their hopes for the
future? Why were they involved? When we consider Lance Corporal Jacinda Baker,
Corporal Luke Tamatea, and Private Richard Harris, we consider not only the next set
of names to be chiselled into those monument s but real people, in our experience, doing
a real and difficult job and paying an awful sacrifice for doing so.
We may all well have our own views a bout the Afghanistan engagement. This
occasion is not the time to air those. This occasion this afternoon is one to pay tribute to
those who have lost their liv es in pursuit of the objectiv es of that mission, and to
acknowledge the validity of th eir service, the courage of their effort, and the genuine
nature of their involvement. Th ere will be other times and other places to debate the
wider defence and political questions.
But today we stand alongside those indivi duals. We stand alongside their colleagues
in Afghanistan—in Bamian—and in New Zeala nd, their families, and their friends. We
stand again alongside th e other families who have lost l oved ones in this conflict, and
for whom the events of the last 2 weeks w ill be the most awful reminder all over again
of their own experience. This occasion this afternoon is one for this Parliament to say to
those who are suffering today that you have our support, you have our sympathy, you
have our encouragement, and you have our gr ateful admiration for the sacrifices that
have been made in the pursuit of the freedom  and the prosperity that we all seek to
enjoy.
May the memories of Lance Corporal Bake r, Corporal Tamatea, and Private Harris
linger for a very long time. May their reputa tions and their honour be proudly displayed
in the annals of our military history. May their families and friends take solace and
comfort from the words of this Parliament this afternoon. May they rest in peace.
Motion agreed to.
Ministers—Appropriate Use of Information
1. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
have confidence in all of his Ministers; if so, why?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes; because they are hard-working
Ministers focused on building a brighter future for New Zealanders.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Did the Minister for Social Deve lopment abuse her power when she
released the personal, private details of an individual?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No. The matter has been looked at by the human rights
director and the case has now been settled.
4534 Questions for Oral Answer 21 Aug 2012

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is he still comfortable, as he said, with his Minister releasing

items.text: I am comfortable with the actions  of the Minister, and that is

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is he confident that the Minister is unlikely, as he put it, to release

gain meet the standard to which he holds Ministers to account?

items.text: If one looks at the politically motivated campaign that was run

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How can the Prime Minister have confidence in the
Minister for Land Information when that Minist er, with plenty of time to prepare, gave
the House seriously erroneous information about a major court case?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As I understand it, the Minister did make an error but he also
came down to the House and corrected that error. That is the normal and standard
procedure, and I remember other members of this House having to make similar

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How can he have confidence in the Minister for Land
Information when the Minister told the Hous e last week that the Overseas Investment
Office was powerless to act while a stay  was placed on four farms owned by May
Wang, yet later told the New Zealand Herald that his officials were working on getting

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am not going to go into the individual details, but I am
confident that the Minister has carried out his duties as required by the law and in a

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You recall the Prime
Minister saying that the Minister for Land Information came down and gave this House
an explanation. You recall very well because  you were involved in the two points of
order—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] No. Order! I am on my feet. [ Interruption]
Order! No. Order! This is question time. [ Interruption] Order! I am on my feet, and the
member is trying to question the answer the Prime Minister gave. The member asked
how the Prime Minister has confidence, gi ven these factors. The Prime Minister
explained in his answer why he  has confidence. That is the end of the answer to that
question. It is in the hands of members the precision of the questions they ask. When
they ask how the Prime Minister can have c onfidence in some Minister, there may be a
whole range of reasons why the Prime Minist er has confidence in a Minister. On this
occasion, I believe that the Prime Minister said he thought the Minister had complied
with the requirements of the law, and that is why he had confidence in him. If the
members want particular answers, they have got to be very particular about the wording
in the questions.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You would know full
well that he came down and he gave an explanation, which, you recall, we allowed to
happen—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] The member will resume his seat.
[Interruption] Order! The member is litigating an answer by way of a point of order.
That is totally outside the Standing Orders of this House. The member has been here
21 Aug 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4535
just as long as I have. He knows that the Standing Orders do not provide for that. The
Prime Minister answered the member’s que stion. The member asked how he can have
confidence in the Minister, given certain  circumstances, and the Prime Minister
answered why he had confidence in the Minister.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How can the Prime Minister have confidence in the
Minister for Land Information on the basis that he came down to the House and gave an
explanation, when that explanation demons trably and palpably was wrong and false in
every respect as to the court case’s timing? How can he have confidence on that basis?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member would really need to direct that at the Minister
involved, but my understanding is that the Minister—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This is the second
week I have asked these same simple questions, and now we are being fobbed off on the
basis that I should ask someone else.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] If the member does not resume his seat while
I am on my feet, he will be leaving this Chamber. I am not going to tolerate it any
further. [Interruption] Order! And the member will stop interjecting. Goodness! This is
Parliament. We have just had a serious deba te about New Zealande rs losing their lives
overseas, and we carry on like spoilt brats. [ Interruption] Order! [ Interruption] Order!
The member will leave the Chamber. [ Interruption] The member will leave the
Chamber, and if he carries on like that, he will be named.
Rt Hon Winston Peters withdrew from the Chamber.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I invite you to look
carefully at what just happened. You invoke d people fighting for freedom, and at the
same time stopped a member asking a question, which was a real one.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Speaker did not stop the member asking the question at
all. The member asked his question, and the Prime Minister started answering it. The
member actually was concerned about the wa y the Prime Minister was answering, and
had the legitimate right to raise a point of order, which he did, but then he sought to use
the point of order the wrong way. What he co uld have done in his point of order was
argue that the Prime Minister was not answ ering the question. I would have had some
sympathy for that, because the question as ked how the Prime Minister could have
confidence in a Minister, and that is someth ing the Prime Minister is responsible for.
But a member has to comply with the Standing  Orders, and I will not tolerate in this
House the point of order process being abused like that. And I will not tolerate members
just answering back from thei r seats. The member has an absolute right to raise a point
of order, but it must be focused on what th e Prime Minister is doing. He could have, in
my view, raised a legitimate point of order because the Prime Minister was starting to
answer in a way that perhaps was not appropr iate. The Prime Minister is responsible for
his confidence in Ministers, and therefore to answer that the question was better directed
at the Minister in question was perhaps not an appropriate answer to a question asking
about the Prime Minister’s confidence. Bu t the member asking the question did not
pursue the point of order correctly. He tr ied to litigate information instead of
questioning the Prime Minister’s answer, and then proceeded to argue with the Chair. I
am simply not going to tolerate that. In th e last few days I have  continued to receive
numerous communications from  members of the public w ho are concerned about the
behaviour in their House. We need to pick up our standards a little. I do not want to turn
this place into some boring place, but we need  to pick up our standards a little, and that
is not the way to do it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am sure you will go in the fullness of time and reflect on
what has taken place this afternoon, as you al ways do. In looking at that tape, I would
4536 Questions for Oral Answer 21 Aug 2012
urge you to look at my answer. The member was asking me a question that really spoke
to the motivations of a Minister as he was answering a question in this House last week.
The point I was making to him was that I was not the person to do that, but I was about
to—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I must not allow any member to litigate even their own
answers. The question—[ Interruption] Order! No, the Prime Mini ster must not do that
either. The member’s question was absolutely in order, because he asked why the Prime
Minister has confidence in  his Minister, given certain  circumstances. That was
absolutely within order to ask the Prime Mi nister that question. And the Prime Minister
perhaps got his answer in the wrong order; perhaps he should have answered why he
has confidence, and then suggested that for the detail of the matte r questions should be
referred to the Minister. That is where I thi nk there could have been a legitimate point
of order raised. But the issue remains that he  will not litigate answers in that manner,
and we will not behave in that manner in the House.
Financial Systems—Stability
2. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Minister of Finance :
What progress has the Government made in  ensuring the stability of New Zealand’s
financial system?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We have made good progress. Non-
performing loans held by banks have fallen to less than 2 percent of total loans. Capital
adequacy has improved as New Zealand households and businesses save more and
borrow less. There is strong growth in retail deposits over the past 18 months, and this
reduces banks’ reliance on funding their lending from overseas. The Government and
the Reserve Bank have taken a number of step s to strengthen regulation of the financial
sector, which puts us in a good position to weather another global banking crisis, should
it eventuate.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What are some of the measures the Government has taken to
strengthen regulations for New Zealand’s financial system?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government picked up the work begun by the previous
Government to overhaul capital market regul ations, established the Financial Markets
Authority, and continued to work to bring the non-bank deposit takers—that is, finance
companies—under the Reserve Bank’s supervision. The Reserve Bank has introduced
new core funding ratios for banks, requiring th em to have 70 percent of their funding
from retail deposits in long-term wholesal e funding. The Basel III capital adequacy
standards will apply from 1 January 2013, re quiring banks to hold higher and better-
quality levels of capital, making them safer and more stable.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What further options is the G overnment considering to further
improve the stability of New Zealand’s financial system and to moderate credit cycles?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government is working with the Reserve Bank and
Treasury to assess whether further so-calle d macro-prudential tools could help to
moderate credit cycles and build additional re silience into the system. Internationally,
these tools include increased capital buffers, adjustment to risk weights by sector, and
restrictions on mortgage lo an-to-value ratios. The Reserve Bank actively monitors
macro-prudential indicators such as credit growth each quarter. If these indicators
suggest that an unsustainable credit boo m is likely, the bank would recommend action.
At present, the bank considers that adjustme nts are not required, be cause credit growth
remains subdued.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What benefits could the use of these extra macro-prudential tools
deliver for the New Zealand economy?
21 Aug 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4537

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is as yet reasonably unclear what benefits they could offer.
Based on modelling work that has been done and international experience, there is some
potential that these tools might moderate rapid increases in bo rrowing. However, there
is no silver bullet. Other policy settings also  have a role to en sure we have price
stability. For instance, we need to ensure that  the Government gets back to surplus, and
that we have sound microeconomic settings  that encourage business investment and
growth.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: If economic settings are important, how can the long-term
financial stability of a financial system  be ensured when 4,337 people a month are
departing for Australia permanently?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The factors that I have outlined  in answer to these questions
are the factors that are generally consider ed, I think rightly so , as those that are
important to financial stability, and financial stability is an important factor for growth.
Those countries that have not had it—that have had unstable financial systems—have
got themselves in a real mess.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: How can the Minister be so sanguine about stability in the
financial system when underlying economic growth is weak, jobs are not being created,
the New Zealand economy is being hollowed ou t, and, as a result, record numbers of
New Zealanders are leaving for Australia—now 162,000 people since he took office?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, the member is mainly incorrect. In fact, by
international standards we ha ve one of the most stable financial systems. We have
moderate growth and new jobs are being created, in contrast to most developed
economies, which continue to shrink. That  is why the Government is publishing its
Business Growth Agenda in order to work with businesses to ensure we build
confidence, build investment, create jobs, and earn higher incomes.

Afghanistan, Bamian—Deployment of Provincial Reconstruction Team
4. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Will he
recommit the provincial reconstruction team to Bamian province in Afghanistan when
the current deployment ends in October; if so, why?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have been clear that the withdrawal of the
provincial reconstruction team from Bamian will take place in 2013. We are continuing
to work on dates for that, alt hough it is likely to be arou nd April. If the member is
asking whether the present rotation will be  replaced with another when the rotation
ends, then the answer is yes. However, I will not be commenting on or confirming the
specific timing of the rotation changes, as is standard practice.
4538 Questions for Oral Answer 21 Aug 2012

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: What work has the Government been doing to develop an exit
strategy for the provincial reconstruction team , given that President Hamid Karzai in
early 2011 called for the withdrawal of the provincial reconstruction teams throughout
Afghanistan?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The Government has been working with the Chief of Defence
Force and the military on the withdrawal pr ogramme. As you are aware, in terms of
Bamian, we are one of the first provincial reconstruction teams to transition out. By
transitioning out in around about April 2013, we will be in line with other, similar
provincial reconstruction teams. We are now working on making sure that the exit of
our 145-plus personnel in Bamian Province is done in the safest way possible for those
particular men and women.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Has the number of troops stati oned in Bamian increased or
decreased since 2010, when the then defen ce Minister, Wayne Mapp, signalled that we
would begin to draw down the provincial reconstruction team from September 2011?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I simply do not have those numbers to hand. I am happy to go
and get those numbers. I can give them to the member.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Will the current provincial reconstruction team deployment all
be withdrawn in the rotation in October, or whenever it happens?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, I think the member need s to make sure he gets his
terminology correct. The deployment is the co mmitment of our forces to Afghanistan.
The rotation is the period of each of th e groups that goes through. If the question is
whether all of them will be replaced, that is  an answer that only the Chief of Defence
Force can give. That is a matter for him to decide—who comes out and who stays in.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: So if we assume that the vast bulk of the current provincial
reconstruction team can be withdrawn in Oct ober, or whatever the date is that the
Government plans to do the rotation, is it necessary to send in another deployment to
replace them?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The advice I have had from the Chief of Defence Force is yes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: What defence equipment in Afghanistan is so vital or difficult
to remove that it will take until 2013 to pack it up?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, there are a number of issu es there. I mean, firstly, we
have three bases in operation in Afghanista n. We have significant bases that need to
remove equipment that, for a variety of reasons , it is not possible nor sensible for us to
leave in Afghanistan. We also  deal with issues around we ather. The member will be
aware that the weather closes in when the snows come in November, and that continues
for a period of time. So, overall, on the best advice we have had, the most probable, and
likely, and sensible date is April 2013.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Prime Minister saying that  we are staying in Afghanistan
past the October, or thereabouts, rotation, because of the logistical reasons or because of
the commitments we have made to the International Security Assistance Force?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is because of a number of reasons. Firstly, we have been on
a transition path that is part of an overall commitment made by all International Security
Assistance Force and NATO countries as th ey exit Afghanistan. So our commitments
are partly for those reasons. Secondly, it is b ecause of logistical r easons. Thirdly, it is
allowing us to finish some of the humanitarian aid efforts that, as we have been pointing
out today, have been hugely successful. So it is a combination of all these things. I think
that if we take a step back, what we can say is that we have been there, as the provincial
reconstruction team, since 2003. We all in this House and across New Zealand mourn
the loss of those 10 soldiers and we pay tribut e to their service, but I think we can also
look with some great pride at the work that they have achieved in those last 8 years or 9
years, and I do not think we would either honour the loss of those individuals or mark
21 Aug 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4539
properly the contribution that New Zealand has made by making a rushed exit for the
door. I think we should do that in a sensible , orderly, and professional way, as has been
the basis of all of our efforts in Afghanist an since Helen Clark sent the SAS there in
2001 and the provincial reconstruction team in 2003.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Without dishonouring those who have fallen in Afghanistan,
does the Government understand  that reducing the risk to  the remaining New Zealand
forces over there could help re duce the risk of any further lo ss of life, and, hence, will
the Government be pulling out of the north-eas t part of the province, which seems to be
the most dangerous part of the deployment?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: First, let me give the member an assurance that the
Government works with the military to make sure that we provide the most safe and
secure environment as we possibly can in Af ghanistan, but put it in  the context of the
fact that this is a war zone. So the Governme nt makes sure that the resources are there,
that the support is there, we are constantly  reviewing what takes place there, and we do
everything we can to provide security and safety, but, unfortunately, we are dealing with
a quite sophisticated insurgent group, which has been very ac tive in recent times. So, in
terms of that, the member can take some c onfidence that we are doing those things. In
terms of the withdrawal of the provincial reconstruction team, that  will be a staged
process, for a variety of different reasons. Bu t at this point I am not in a position to
detail exactly the timing of the different stages as we pack up various different camps
and bases that we have.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Will the Prime Minister accept the Labour Party’s support for an
orderly transition of the forces out of Afghanistan as promptly as possible?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am more than happy to give the member a briefing on all the
things that are taking place, the reasons fo r why we are going through this process, and
why it is the belief of the Chief of Defen ce Force and the military that the programme
that we are on to withdraw is  the right one. I think, to be  frank, we have worked in a
spirit of cooperation for a very long period of  time with the Labour Party on this issue,
as I think National did in Opposition, and we are more than happy to inform the
member of the rationale for what is happe ning and why we are doing what we are
doing. Some of that information is confid ential and we cannot put it in the public
domain, but we respect the member’s word  and he would, obviously, appreciate that
information. If he and the Opposition defence spokesman want to have a briefing, then I
am happy to have that arranged by the Chief of Defence Force.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Has his Government changed the mandate of the provincial
reconstruction team, given that when they were first deployed under the Helen Clark
Government in 2003, the then defence Minister , Mark Burton, stated very clearly that
they were not a “combat unit”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not have the original manda te that the member speaks of
to hand, so I cannot comment about whether there are differences from those ones or the
ones that my Government has rolled over as  each rotation has gone through. But what I
can say is that the provincial reconstructio n team does a variety of  different tasks in
Bamian, and for the most part those have b een engagement with and working with the
local community, working on areas of develo pment, but there has always been an
element of providing security for our humanitarian aid efforts, so that those workers can
carry on the great works that we have seen. As I noted today, I think we can be very
proud of some of those efforts. We now ha ve a situation where half of all primary
school children who go to school in Bamian are girls; there is a multi-faculty institution,
Bamian University, with 2,700 people there, in operation; and the mortality rate for
children under 5 has almost halved. So I th ink the men and women of whom there are a
very large number who have now served in  that provincial reconstruction team since
4540 Questions for Oral Answer 21 Aug 2012
2003 deserve the congratulations of this country on the effort s and the work that they
have done, and I hope that in the years to come it will bear fruit for the people of
Bamian.
Social Development, Minister—Statements
5. JACINDA ARDERN (Labour)  to the Minister for Social Development : Does
she stand by all of her statements?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Yes, although I do
have a tendency to get a li ttle over-exuberant at times, as, Mr Speaker, you witnessed
last week.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Has she shared with the Prime Mini ster her statement, as quoted in
the media, that she could in future releas e the personal details of those who receive
Government support “depending on the circumstances”; if so, what was his response?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I spoke to the Prime Minister on Sunday on a range of
issues to do with my portfolio, and it came up in  that conversation. He sort of asked me
to catch him up on what had been happening last  week, and I said to him that I have not
disclosed any further information in the last  3 years, I do not intend on doing it next
week, and I do not intend on doing it next m onth, but I cannot give a guarantee around
every circumstance. It is what I said last week, it is what I said on Sunday to him, and it
is what I still say today.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Does she agree with the Prime Minister’s pos ition, as outlined to
the media, that her release of the private in formation of two individuals on Government
support was wrong?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I have actually read the Prime Minister’s transcript from
yesterday and that is not what he said.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Did the Prime Minister ask her not  to share the private information
of people on Government support in the future?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Absolutely not.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I call Jacinda Ardern—[ Interruption] Order! I want to hear Jacinda
Ardern.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Did the Prime Minister express to  her in their discussion that he
agreed with her actions in re leasing the information of tw o individuals on Government
support?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I think I have reiterated to the best of my ability the
conversation I had with the Prime Minister on Sunday. I understand that those members
are trying to get some great conspiracy th eory, but it was quite straightforward. We
were merely having quite a catch-up. He asked me to tell him about—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: He just ticked you off.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: No, I never got a telling o ff. I know what a telling off
looks like after last week, and it certainly was nothing like that. It was actually quite
clear that we were having a conversation about  what was going on. I said to him, as I
am happy to reiterate to you, th at I have not disclosed info rmation in the last 3 years
since then, I do not intend on doing it next week, I do not intend on doing it next month,
but I just cannot give every permutation of circumstances that might come up and give
an absolute guarantee that nothing might ha ppen. He simply accepted that and, I think,
reiterated that yesterday at his press conference.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: During her catch-up with the Prime Minister did he agree with her
that children move in and out of poverty on a daily basis?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Like me, the Prime Minister would have seen the
Treasury report that does a de scriptive analysis of income  and deprivation. He would
have seen that from 2002 to 2009 only 24 per cent of people stayed in the lowest income
21 Aug 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4541
deprivation—that 76 percent actually moved. I can quote from it if it would help the
member: “The mobility is both up and down, though there is more for the bottom
deciles than the top deciles—only 24% of t hose in the bottom decile in 2002 were also
there in 2009,” showing that more than 75 percent actually move around.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does she accept that her statement that she reserves the right to
go to the files and release the private inform ation of people who disagree with her can
have a chilling effect on free speech in a democratic society?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: See, I do not think that information was disclosed simply
because someone disagreed with me. I am  not going to reiter ate yet again what
happened at that point, but by no means is that my interpretation. In my letter I made the
point that people should be free to speak in this country and that I support democracy. I
stand by that with every inch of what I have got.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Can she confirm that the Treasury  report she has quoted indicated
movement between low income and poverty on a daily or a yearly basis?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I think it is quite clear that people move, whether it be on
a particular day or on an annual basis. Wh at you have is mobility of income. I think
what the member does not get is that we on this side are not deciding whether we dream
up another measure of poverty, whether it is 10 percent or 20 percent—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It was a very direct
question about the specific Treasury report from which the Minister was quoting. We
have not had even an attempt to respond to that yet.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Well, with respect, I believe the Minister did answer it. She argued
that the Treasury report indicates that chil dren can move on a give n day, over a year, or
whatever. That is how the Minister answer ed the question. The question asked whether
the report showed children could move on a daily basis, and it seems to be the
Minister’s interpretation from her answer that she believes it does.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The question was about
the Treasury report and the response was either—I cannot remember her words—“I
believe” or “we believe”. It had nothing to do with what was in the report.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Oh, no, no. The Minister, if I recollect correctly, did refer to the
Treasury report in answering the question. It is a matter, it would seem, of interpretation
of the Treasury report. I cannot judge that, but I have to take  the Minister at her word.
She said the Treasury report indicates childre n moving on different ba ses. It could be

Business Growth Agenda—Building Innovation Progress Report and Funding for
Research and Development
6. COLIN KING (National—Kaik ōura) to the Minister of Science and

items.speaker: Innovation
items.text: What announcements has he made re garding the Government’s work to
boost innovation?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: This morning,
alongside the Prime Minister and the Mini ster for Communications and Information
Technology, I released the Building Innovation progress report, which is the second of
six reports being released by the Government detaili ng and updating our Business
Growth Agenda. The Building Innovation report outlines more than 50 current and new
Government initiatives across the innovation space. Specific measures include further
information on the Advanced Technology Institute, including that it will be named after
the late Sir Paul Callaghan; the launchi ng of National Science Challenges, asking the
public to assist us to identify New Zeala nd’s greatest challenges, and working with
researchers to achieve innovative solutions; encouraging the development of innovation
parks, which involves clustering research prov iders with innovative private sector firms
and start-ups to take advantage of having highly skilled scien tists and innovators
working in close proximity; a nd developing a small advanced  economies initiative with
similar sized and advanced nations to fo cus on how we can use science and innovation
to position for economic growth.

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: How will the Government assist  business to boost research and
development?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Government has set an ambitious target to increase
private sector research and developmen t funding—double from 0.54 percent to more
than 1 percent. To help business achieve these goals, we have greatly increased the
TechNZ co-funding for businesses to $115 million per year in 2012-13. We have
committed to the Primary Growth Partners hip combining Government and industry
investment worth $600 million, of which aroun d half comes from the Government. We
have committed $166 million over the next  4 years to develop the Advanced
Technology Institute. We have a project wo rking to ensure we obtain the maximum
leverage from Government funding in te rms of increased firm research and
development. And we are also examining ways to improve the incubator model to
21 Aug 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4543
ensure more start-ups have the opportunity  to commercialise their ideas and launch
products.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

items.text: How is that possible?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: —because questions that are straig ht questions must be dealt with
with integrity. If there is a political load ing in a question or statements that have

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. I appreciate that you

4544 Questions for Oral Answer 21 Aug 2012

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

Health Targets—Cancer Treatment
8. Dr JACKIE BLUE (National)  to the Minister of Health: What progress can he
report on improvements to cancer services?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I can report that the Government will
invest $16 million over the next 4 years to ensu re that every district health board can
provide its patients with the care of dedi cated cancer coordinati on nurses. All up, 40
dedicated cancer coordination nurses will be  working in health boards throughout the
country by the end of the year. These specialist nurses will act as a single point of
contact so that patients and their families no longer have to deal with navigating through
multiple people from different parts of the health service throughout their treatment. It is
expected that the district health boards will  begin advertising vacancies for these roles
in the next couple of months.

items.speaker: Dr Jackie Blue
items.text: What evidence is there that this money will make a difference?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The concept is modelled on the successful work of a number
of nurses around New Zealand, particularly the cancer c linical specia lists at the
Canterbury District Health Board, and in the New South Wales health service, which is
found to have a high impact on the services for cancer patie nts. Incredibly, during a
cancer patient’s treatment they can deal with  up to 28 different doctors and many more
different nurses. These dedicated cancer coordination nurses will coordinate and
improve the quality of care for patients and provide them with a personal point of
contact for information and support. This was part of the $33 million Budget
announcement in respect of cancer made a few months ago by the Prime Minister.

Welfare Reforms—Initiatives Targeting At-risk Young People
10. Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA (National—Maungakiekie) to the Minister for

items.speaker: Social Development
items.text: How is the Government bette r supporting young people who are
either on a benefit or not engaged in education, training or employment?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: This week marks the
start of the Government’s comprehensiv e youth services for disengaged young people.
More than $148 million in wraparound suppo rt services will help young people on
benefit off benefit, and those at risk of going on benefit, as well. Each young person will
be allocated a service provider, who will manage their benefit payments, provide
mentoring support, have an unwavering em phasis on education and training, and, for
those with children, also help them with parenting courses.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: How have these services been targeted to ensure they reach
those young people who are most at risk of long-term welfare dependency?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The new youth services are for 16 and 17-year-olds and
16 to 18-year-old teen parent s on benefit, and will also target up to 14,000 teenagers
aged 16 and 17 who are not in education, em ployment, or training. We have targeted
these young people as for the first time we actually know who is going on benefit and
the kinds of services we need so that we can put them on a different path in life.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Does the Minister accept that the contract to address the numbers of
young people not in education, employment, or  training north of Auckland, all the way
to Te Hana, going to an out-of-area provi der has now significantly disadvantaged and
competes with successful community provi ders previously working with these young

Family Centre of Helensville; if so, what will she do to address this consequence?

conversations with these service provide rs, of which there are 42 throughout the
country, to see where they can partner with ot her providers in other areas. So they are
saying that they are talking to  other providers to see that. There are also, as has been
identified by the Opposition quite often, ki ds who are 18 years and older who are
needing services, and, actually, Springboard and others like it are addressing the needs
of those young people, as well. So I do think we  can cover it, and I do not think it needs
to be to the detriment of the services the member mentions.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: What role would the commun ity youth service providers
have?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: We have selected actually 43. I think I said 42 in answer

which is already under way and making a difference.

items.text: Can the Minister confirm for the House that in no instance where a

items.text: I reiterate: I do not have access to private information

Afghanistan—Provincial Reconstruction Team and Deaths of Army Personnel

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received a letter from Dr Russel Norman seeking to debate
under Standing Order 386 the deaths of thr ee New Zealand personnel serving in the
provincial reconstruction team in Afgha nistan on Sunday, 19 August, the range of
operations of the provincial reconstruction team, the equipment used by the provincial
reconstruction team, and the withdrawal date of the provincial reconstruction team.
The deaths of the New Zealand personnel is a particular case of recent occurrence of
grave concern to New Zeala nd and involving ministerial re sponsibility. However, the
House has more appropriate ways of rec ognising such events and has today already
done so. The urgent debate procedure is a means of debating matters that have occurred.
The accumulation of information or continui ng issues do not meet the test of a
particular case of recent occurrence. A de bate occurs at the point in time when a
decision is publicly announced. No decision on a withdrawal date has yet been made,
and the range of operations and the equipmen t used by the provin cial reconstruction
team are ongoing operational matters.
It is also relevant, when considering whether a matter requires the urgent attention of
the House, to consider whether there are other parliamentary means of debating the
subject. The House has before it today th e third reading of th e Appropriation (2012/13
Estimates) Bill, which may be taken with an Imprest Supply Bill. As is the case with the
Address in Reply debate and the Budget debate, there is vi rtually no limitation on the
debate on such a bill on the grounds of relevancy. This provides an opportunity today to
debate the ongoing operations  and the possible timing of any withdrawal. The
application is therefore declined.
